title: The herbs that hid
hookLine: a night flight the length of India, and herbs that hide
carry: the healing plants are alive, and holy
last: SANKAT MOCHAN: IN TROUBLE, CALL ON HANUMAN.

cards: Hanuman climbs a mountain at the edge of the sea to push off, and he grows, the way he grew before the first leap. He presses down with his feet, and the mountain buckles under him. Then he's in the air, heading north.
This isn't the hop to Lanka. This is the whole length of India, there and back, before dawn, with the army lying in the dark behind him.

teach.h: THE LENGTH OF INDIA AT NIGHT.
teach.b: Valmiki lets us ride along. Below him slide the ocean, then forests, rivers and towns, the hermitages of sages, the land unrolling under a flying monkey at night. Then the Himalaya rise ahead, snow and gold and rock.
He sees Kailasa, the home of Shiva. He sees Mount Rishabha.
And between them, just as Jambavan said, the mountain of herbs, glowing with its plants. Then the twist. Hanuman searches the slopes, and he can't find the four herbs.
Valmiki says the plants knew someone had come for them, and hid; they made themselves invisible. The clock is running. Hanuman gets angry and speaks to the mountain: you won't help Rama?

He grips the whole peak, with its trees, its animals, its glowing herbs, tears it loose, and flies south with it, shining like a second sun. If you've grown up seeing Hanuman's picture, this is the one.
But look at the detail Valmiki slips in: the herbs knew. In this story, plants aren't just things. They sense, they hide, they heal.

teach.h: THE HEALING PLANTS ARE ALIVE, AND HOLY.
teach.b: The Rig Veda has a whole hymn to the healing plants, calling them mothers and goddesses.
And in many Hindu homes today, a tulsi plant, holy basil, grows in a pot by the door, watered each morning, a lamp lit beside it in the evening, honored as a goddess dear to Vishnu.
When Hanuman spoke to that mountain, he was speaking to something alive.

how: Many Hindu homes keep a tulsi plant, watered daily and honored with a lamp; images of Hanuman flying with a mountain on his hand are found in temples, homes and calendars across India.

games.q: what does “the mountain of herbs” mean?
o: a hill in Lanka where Ravana keeps his healers
the mountain the monkeys use to build the bridge
the Himalayan peak Hanuman lifts when its herbs hide

games.q: the flight north — tap the pairs.

s: the Rig Veda has a hymn to the healing plants
it praises them as mothers and goddesses.
Valmiki says the herbs hid when they knew someone had come
the demon Kalanemi's trap on the way is in Valmiki
that episode comes from later tellings, such as the Ramcharitmanas.

games.q: nani asks you to pick a few tulsi leaves for the evening puja. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: grab a handful. it's just basil.
pick a few gently, with thanks, as from something alive and holy.
games.why: Hindus treat tulsi as holy, and many families pick its leaves with care and a short prayer. like the herbs on the mountain, it's alive.

practice: Find a plant near you, or picture one. Many Hindu families offer water to their tulsi each morning. If you pray, pour a little water at its roots, or imagine it, with a quiet thanks to God for the life in it.
If you don't, give it water and one full minute of attention, the way you'd visit someone alive.

wordCard.voice: The mountain of herbs. A peak in the Himalaya whose healing plants knew Hanuman had come and hid, so he carried the whole mountain south.

orig.note: Sanskrit oṣadhi: a healing plant or herb; the herb mountain is the oṣadhi-parvata.

carryVoice: Your line: the healing plants are alive, and holy. The landing comes next, and a scent on the wind. Day six hundred forty-nine, done.
